Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:35: And the end of his words there teaches you that no good comes from wine. In particular, students of Torah must be careful about excess wine, for wine brings sleep, and our Sages of blessed memory said in Sanhedrin (8:5), "wine and sleep for the wicked are good for them and good for the world; for the righteous, bad for them and bad for the world" — for wine harms the righteous because it increases sleep and causes them to become idle from words of Torah. This is why King Solomon, peace be upon him, after disparaging wine, praised wisdom, saying (Proverbs 24:1), "Do not envy evil men, nor desire to be with them" etc., and then said (ibid. 24:3), "Through wisdom is a house built," and said (ibid. 24:5), "A wise man is strengthened by might, and a man of knowledge strengthens power," and then said (ibid. 24:6), "If you falter in a day of trouble, your strength is small." Our Sages said in Midrash Mishlei on this verse, Rabbi Abahu said: whoever weakens himself from words of Torah has no strength to stand on a day of trouble. In the Zohar, portion Vayetze (152b), they elaborated on the interpretation of this verse, and we shall copy it in its place. Thus we find that for a Torah scholar, wine is a cause that weakens him from words of Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:36: And you will find that they said in the Mishnah (Ta'anit 2:7) that the men of the watch were permitted to drink wine at night but not by day, while the men of the father's house [officiating that day] neither by day nor by night. Rashi explained: at night, there was no concern that the service would become burdensome, since they saw already in the evening that the offerings had ceased and the service was not heavy. Not by day, because most of the offerings would come and the men of the father's house alone would not suffice for that whole day, and these others would need to assist them, and they would not be fit for service on account of intoxication. The men of the father's house, whether by day or night, since they would be lifting up all night the limbs and fats that had slipped off the altar, or if they had not finished by day, they would finish at night — but the men of the watch did not need to assist at night in turning with the fork, since the father's house alone could manage the turning of the arrangement. Thus far his words. We find, then, that whoever had heavy service upon them was forbidden wine so that they would not become idle from the service. Likewise, one who wishes to bear the yoke of Torah and not become idle from it should distance himself from wine.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:37: And they said in Midrash HaNe'elam (Zohar, portion Vayera, beginning of 110), these are their words: Rabbi Yitzchak said, the evil inclination is never enticed except through eating and drinking, and through the joy of wine it then rules over a person. Of the righteous, what is written of him? (Proverbs 13:25) "The righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul," and he never becomes drunk, for Rabbi Yehuda said: a young Torah scholar who becomes drunk — of him is it read (ibid. 11:22), "A gold ring in a pig's snout," and moreover, he profanes the Name of Heaven. What is the practice of the wicked? "Behold joy and gladness" (Isaiah 22:13) — wine then rules over a person — "slaying oxen and killing sheep" etc. (ibid.), and of them the verse says (Isaiah 5:11), "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink," in order to arouse the evil inclination, for the evil inclination is aroused only through wine, as it is said (Genesis 19:33), "and they gave their father wine to drink." Thus far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:38: And regarding the intent of eating and drinking according to the plain meaning, Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, wrote in the book Menorat HaMaor, that one must be happy with his portion, and trust in his Maker that He will provide his sustenance, and not restrict himself with the minutiae of poverty. And so they said in the Midrash, "all the days of the poor are evil" — meaning, one who is poor in his faith and is distressed over expense; and if he does acquire sustenance for himself, he fears that he will decline from his possessions and become dependent on others — thus all his days are in sorrow and worry. But one who is happy with his portion and believes in the Holy One, blessed be He, that He provides his sustenance whenever he needs it, his heart is always glad and good, as though a table were forever set and a feast forever before him. And further we learn in the Midrash, "Better a dry morsel with tranquility" etc. (Proverbs 17:1) — this refers to one happy with his portion, who is always at ease and calm, since he is happy with what the Holy One, blessed be He, has provided him; he will never steal or rob, and is found tranquil and secure all his days. "Than a house full of feasting with strife" — this refers to one who is not happy with his portion, but pursues coarse foods, and steals and robs to satisfy his desire, and is found all his days in strife and quarrel, pursued by people. But one who eats a little to the satisfaction of his soul and does not intend the pleasure of his body — he recognizes his Creator, for when he hungers he will understand his own deficiency and the lowliness of man, for when he lacks bread and a cup of water, his strength and all his limbs weaken, his eyes darken, and he cannot muster strength to stand on his feet; and then he recognizes the perfection of the Holy One, blessed be He, who needs neither food nor drink, as it is said (Psalms 50:13), "Do I eat the flesh of bulls" etc. And when he hungers he lifts his eyes to the Holy One, blessed be He, to seek his sustenance, and knows that He, blessed be His Name, gives bread to all flesh, and provides sustenance to each and every one, and to every body its sufficiency of need. And then he has compassion on the poor and distances himself from arrogance, since coarse foods bring a person to sins and guilt, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:15), "And Jeshurun grew fat and kicked," and it is written (ibid. 11:15), "and you shall eat and be satisfied, take heed to yourselves" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:39: And what is praiseworthy in a person regarding eating are three things. First, that he be content with his portion even if it is little, and not seek more. Second, that he eat at his proper time, before he becomes very hungry and his limbs weaken and he comes to illness, so that he lacks the strength to serve the Holy One, blessed be He, properly, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 10:16), "and your princes eat in the proper time." Third, that he not intend in his eating the pleasure of his body but only the sustenance of his soul, and not follow his desire to eat everything the palate craves of bad foods, since they cause harm. And Ramban, of blessed memory, wrote: a person should always reduce his eating by a third. And they said (Gittin 70a): a meal from which you derive pleasure, withdraw your hands from it. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:40: And the pious one in Chovot HaLevavot, of blessed memory (Gate of Abstinence, ch. 5), wrote regarding abstinence in eating, these are his words: it is fitting for you, my brother, that you conduct yourself with abstinence from the permitted pleasures within your ability, until they appear in your eyes like the nature of pleasures forbidden to you — meaning like milk [with meat] and the like — lest you abandon your Torah and neglect your duty. And you have already noted what the Creator, blessed be He, commanded the king, saying (Deuteronomy 17:17), "he shall not multiply wives for himself," and He said (ibid. 17:16), "only he shall not multiply horses for himself," and it is said (cf. Nehemiah 13:26), "was it not for these that King Solomon sinned," despite all the strength of his intellect and abundance of his understanding and greatness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:41: And he further said below: strive to restrain the sense of taste, so that you take from food and drink only what suffices for your nourishment, and abstain from what is more than this. The strategy for this matter is that you minimize the varieties of relish, and rely on a single relish as long as you are able, and likewise accustom your soul at certain times to go without relish altogether, in order to train your stomach and your nature, until the matter becomes easy for you when you must forgo it. And if you can forgo relish that requires labor and toil, and rely instead on what requires no labor at all, such as olives, figs, grapes, and the like, do so, and make your daytime eating lighter than your nighttime eating, if it is your custom to eat many times during the day, so that the movement of your limbs be light by day and the affairs of your Torah and your worldly matters be easy for you.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:42: And afterward accustom yourself to fasting of the body, if your body is strong, even one day a week, and whatever you are able to train your soul not to feel regarding food and drink in order to discipline it, do so, and direct your intent in it toward healing rather than nourishment; and let all your drinking be water, unless your intent in wine is to drink for the benefit of your body or to remove worry from your heart, as it is said (Proverbs 31:6), "Give strong drink to him who is perishing." But beware of increasing it and indulging in it, and of the company of people gathered over it, for it is the great malady for Torah and for the world. The Sage has already told of it what suffices (Proverbs 20:1), "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is riotous," and he said regarding food and drink (ibid. 23:20), "Be not among winebibbers" etc., "for the glutton and the drunkard shall come to poverty" etc. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:43: And this path that the pious one, of blessed memory, wrote is the path of abstinence fitting for masters of Torah whose main occupation is Torah; for if a master of Torah wishes to rely on trust in God yet spend his money on eating meat or chickens and similar kinds of pleasures, he will find himself burdened with the affairs of this world in pursuit of his provisions, and will become idle from words of Torah, and when he does not find his accustomed fare he will be unable to bear it and will fall ill. Therefore it is fitting that every Torah scholar conduct himself with this abstinence that is written in Chovot HaLevavot.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:44: And likewise there are several statements from our Sages supporting this, distancing pleasures from masters of Torah. Among them, first, the beraita of the Acquisition of Torah (Avot 6:4-5): "Such is the way of Torah: bread with salt shall you eat" etc., "do not crave the table of kings." And our father Jacob, peace be upon him, asked only for "bread to eat and clothing to wear" (Genesis 28:20). And in this are fulfilled the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, who said (portion Terumah, 141a): fortunate is one who takes no pleasure at all for himself. And especially if he eats only for healing, as the pious one, of blessed memory, wrote, this is the most praiseworthy standard — that he derives no pleasure at all for himself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:45: And likewise it is fitting for one who wishes to sanctify himself that he eat only for healing, so that he not become ill and become idle from Torah and from the commandments. Therefore it is fitting that he not fill his soul with coarse foods, and even from good things he should not fully satisfy his appetite, even on Shabbat, for excessive eating causes increased sleep, as they said in the first chapter of Yoma (44), "they did not feed him much, for food brings sleep." And when he trains himself to be content with little, he will find rest for his soul, and will sanctify himself in Torah, and will not become distracted while studying.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:46: And the wise man should take this matter to heart, and abstain from his appetite, and not fill his belly and his craving like an animal, for "who is mighty? He who conquers his inclination" (Avot 4:1); and if his inclination entices him to eat, let him break his strength and conquer it from his craving, and then awe and holiness will rest upon him, as it is written (Psalms 34:10), "Fear the LORD, His holy ones."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:47: And likewise Ra'avad wrote in Sha'ar HaKedushah, these are his words: and I see that the great fence, the excellent safeguard, and the good path for subduing the inclination, is hunger of the soul from minimizing its pleasures and enjoyments in food and drink — except that he may enjoy a pleasant scent and the washing of warm water, since warm water is pleasant to him — and the small amount of food he eats should be well-seasoned and prepared nicely, so that it be pleasant to him, and his soul will accept it and be content with a small amount of it. And he should always leave a bit less than his full need and the completion of his desire, and he should not drink wine except well diluted, so that his mind not become disturbed by it. On this path they said (Gittin 70a): a meal from which you derive pleasure, withdraw your hand from it. And there are two great remedies in this: the first, that its eating not harm him; the second, the subduing of the inclination and the breaking of desire. And just as we have said regarding a meal, so is the path for all the world's pleasures and enjoyments — that a person not fill himself with all his desires from them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:48: And needless to say, a person should guard himself from foods he knows to be harmful to him, for one who eats things that harm him when he could avoid them is guilty against his own body and guilty against his own soul, since he follows his desire and disregards the loss of his body — and this is the way of the evil inclination and its foolish counsel to entice him from the way of life to the way of death. And let every living, speaking being know that the evil inclination has no way to him except through the way of the permitted, and its path opens from what is permitted to him; and if he guards that gateway, he need not guard any other.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:49: And I have already laid it all before you at the beginning of this gate: that the way of that wicked counselor is to advise him to fill his desire from what is permitted to him, and after accustoming him to filling his desire through the permitted, and inducing his soul to be perpetually restless and yearning for its indulgence, it entices him to a light prohibition, and from the light to the severe, as I have said. Therefore be careful with the permitted, and if you fence yourself in with it and minimize your desire from what is permitted to you, you are assured that your inclination will no longer entice you toward the forbidden; for if a matter of prohibition should arise, you immediately reason a kal vachomer within yourself: "if I forbade myself what is permitted to me, how much more so what is forbidden to me." And since you carry this kal vachomer upon yourself, you are assured that you abstain even from the mere thought, and certainly from the deed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:50: And a person should not afflict himself with self-mortification, lest he weaken his heart and his deeds and his nature become corrupted, his mind become confused, and his loss exceed his gain, for he will become idle from Torah and from prayer; and if he does study, his Torah will not be settled, and he will not agree upon the halakhah and the analysis of the tradition, since Torah is acquired only from the root of joy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:51: And a person should not deprive himself of any joy of a commandment or any pleasure of a commandment, only that his eyes be open against the inclination, and he be careful lest he fill all his desires. And if his heart weakens from reducing his eating, it is better for him to eat twice a day, a little at a time, and not fill his belly all at once; and if it is not possible for him to eat twice a day, let him keep with him some heart-settling remedies, and eat a little of them so his heart is strengthened. Also, if he sees within himself and by his nature that he needs to fast a day or two, let him fast according to his constitution, for one who sits in fast and needs it is called holy — provided he does not become idle from Torah or from the commandments because of it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:52: Also, an oath, though it is severe, was permitted in order to fence oneself in the time of transgression, as Boaz said regarding Ruth (Ruth 3:13), "As the LORD lives, lie down until morning." Our Sages of blessed memory said (Vayikra Rabbah 23:11) that his inclination argued with him all night, saying to him, "you are unattached and she is unattached, and a woman is acquired through intercourse — go and have relations with her and she will be acquired to you through intercourse." Boaz sprang up and swore against the inclination, "As the LORD lives, lie down until morning" — he swore to the inclination that he would not do this, and to the woman, "lie down until morning." So every person can know for himself which fence is better for him, whether subjugation or the oath. And I see that nothing is better than subjugation and hunger of the soul, as I have said; and if he still needs the oath, let him swear and fulfill it, as David said (Psalms 119:106), "I have sworn, and I will fulfill it, to keep Your righteous judgments." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:53: And I, the lowly one, say that this path is good for one who is able and has the means to purchase remedies; but one who is poor and lacks the means to conduct himself in this manner should at least conduct his eating according to medical guidance, as Rambam wrote in Hilkhot De'ot (ch. 4), that a person should minimize his eating, for this is the correct path. In particular, one who does not fast should minimize his morning meal so as not to become idle from occupation with Torah, and should estimate that his measure of eating be divided between two times, morning and evening, in the amount he was accustomed to being satisfied with in one sitting.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:54: And for one who wishes to persist in rising at midnight to engage in Torah, let him place his main eating at the morning meal, and at night eat only fruits — and let them be dried fruits such as raisins, almonds, walnuts, and figs. Let him distance himself at night from eating coarse foods such as cheese and the like; rather let him conduct himself as Ra'avad wrote above at the beginning of his words, that he eat a small amount, well-seasoned and prepared nicely, and let the bread be less than the cooked food. And for one who wishes to read most of the night, it is good that he not eat bread at all at night — and so my teacher, peace be upon him, was accustomed to do when he was not fasting. And a penitent who is accustomed to fasting every day, on days when he does eat, such as Rosh Chodesh and Yom Tov, should conduct himself in the manner we have written.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:55: And for one for whom the path that Ra'avad, peace be upon him, wrote for the correction of the day is possible, it is good for the correction of the night as well — that he eat nothing at night except heart-settling remedies, and in this way he will be able to stand most of the night engaged in Torah without sleep. Thus he bears a measure of affliction, and does not pursue pleasures, for Torah endures only in one who distances himself from pleasure, as they said in the Zohar (portion Pinchas, 247a) on the verse (cf. Numbers 28:5), "fine flour mingled with crushed oil," explaining there that "fine flour" is the Shechinah, "mingled with oil" — this refers to oil that flows and issues from above. And afterward it says: the Faithful Shepherd said, holy lamp, how sweet are your words! Surely it is said here "mingled with crushed oil," and it was said there [elsewhere] that the Oral Torah is mingled with Scripture, with Mishnah, and with Gemara etc. And there is a second secret: "mingled with crushed oil" — surely the Torah is not "mingled" except for one who bears many poundings for its sake, as the masters of the Mishnah established, that Torah endures only in one who puts himself to death over it. And further it says: at the time you wear out your feet from city to city, you will merit to see the face of the Shechinah. And further, "mingled with crushed oil" — this is what fulfills "bread with salt shall you eat, and water by measure shall you drink." And further, "mingled with crushed oil," this is what is written (Isaiah 53:5), "and he was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:56: Behold, it is explicit that the Torah, called "fine flour," does not endure in a person unless he pounds himself and puts himself to death, fulfilling "bread with salt shall you eat." And even though it says "and further," all these interpretations arrive at the same point — that the intent is the pounding of matter so that the Torah and the soul shine within it, and this is the path to attaining Torah, that even if he is wealthy he should not indulge himself in pleasures. This is what is meant by "such is the way of Torah" etc. (Avot 6:4), and this is what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 119:71), "It is good for me that I was afflicted, so that I might learn Your statutes."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:57: And it says in the Zohar (portion Bereshit, 11a) that when Rashbi, peace be upon him, and Rabbi Elazar came out of the cave, Rabbi Pinchas went to see him. It says: he went to him and found him repeating Mishnayot, his body full of sores; he wept together with him and said, "woe that I see you thus." He said, "fortunate is my portion that you see me thus, for had you not seen me thus, I would not be thus." Thus far his words. And likewise they said in the Gemara, tractate Shabbat (33b). It is thus explicit that through the sufferings he bore in the cave he attained wondrous wisdom, and likewise they said in Tana d'Bei Eliyahu that during the thirteen years Rashbi, peace be upon him, was confined in the cave, the depths of wisdom were revealed to him and he attained knowledge of future things.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:58: And especially one who has sins must bear sufferings for his sins and will not merit the supernal light, which is the oil of which David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 23:5), "You have anointed my head with oil," unless he pounds himself. And this is what is meant by "and further, mingled with crushed oil, this is what is written (Isaiah 53:5), 'and he was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities'" — the intent being that just as the Messiah suffers, our sins cause him to be crushed; so if one wishes that the Messiah not be crushed on account of our sins, let him bear suffering and crush himself. And so they explained in Sefer Chasidim (§528), that a certain pious man bore several sufferings for his sins and gave this reason mentioned; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:59: Further, in Tana d'Bei Eliyahu, cited in the Yalkut, portion Va'etchanan (§830, 265c), on the verse "I am the LORD your God" — these are his words: a person does not merit that Torah enter his innards unless he seeks mercy that excessive eating and drinking not enter his innards, as it is said (Isaiah 48:10), "I have refined you, but not with silver; I have tested you in the furnace of affliction." Just as this furnace — even if you put into it all the wood in the world — burns and destroys it, so too the throat of a person — even if you give him all the foods in the world, he destroys them. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:60: Further they said in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 19:1): Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said, words of Torah require blackening and darkening [of oneself]. Whence sustenance? "Who prepares for the raven its prey?" (Job 38:41) — so too, unless a person becomes cruel to himself, to his children, and to his household like this raven, he does not merit words of Torah. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:61: And the reason that Torah dwells in a person only after he distances pleasures from himself, is because Torah is called holy, as it is said (Proverbs 2:5), "and you will find the knowledge of God," and therefore it dwells only in a place where there is holiness and abstinence from bodily pleasures.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:62: And Rabbi Yisrael, of blessed memory, wrote in the book Menorat HaMaor: great is the Torah, for so great is its holiness that even from bread and water Moses had to sanctify himself before he received the Torah, as it is said (Exodus 34:28), "and he was there with the LORD." And is this not a kal vachomer: if from bread and water, which are pure, he sanctified himself forty days, how much more so must we sanctify ourselves for words of Torah from all impurity. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:63: And it seems to me, regarding the intent of eating, as understood from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, what he explained in the Zohar (portion Terumah, 154b), that there is a supernal table upon which is the shewbread, and he said: from the secret of this table sustenance issues to the world, in accordance with what is given into it from above; and that bread is the fruit and sustenance issuing from this table — to show that from this table issue fruits, produce, and sustenance for the world. If there were no vineyard, the grapes that are its fruit issuing from it would not be found; if there were no tree, its fruit would not be found in the world. For this reason, the table is the principal thing, and the sustenance issuing from it is that bread.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:64: And he said further below: a person's table must be found in bodily cleanliness, that he not approach to eat his sustenance except in his own cleanliness. For this reason a person must first empty himself before he eats the sustenance of the pure table, for that sustenance he prepares — the Holy One, blessed be He, delights in it, since one may not bring near to that table vomit and excrement, which is from the secret of the Other Side, and the Other Side should receive nothing at all from the sustenance of this table. After a person eats and enjoys, he must give a portion of the residue to that Side. And what is it? Mayim acharonim [the final washing of hands after a meal] — that filth of the hands which must be given to that Side its needed portion. This is certainly guilt, and it rests where guilt rests, and it is an obligation upon a person to give it this portion; therefore no blessing at all is required over it, for blessing does not belong to that Side. For this reason a person must not give the sustenance upon his table to that vomit and excrement, and all the more so within his innards, and all the more so that this is good for a person and for the health and correction of his body. Therefore the table is for eating upon it in purity, as has been said. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:65: Now, from the reason given in this statement — that it is forbidden to give a portion of one's sustenance to that vomit and excrement — we may also understand the reason for (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul." The reason is: since this sustenance is hinted to issue from the supernal table, it is not fitting that the external [forces] have a share in it — that which is called vomit and excrement. And just as it is done physically, so is it done spiritually: from the supernal sustenance the soul certainly benefits, and therefore it is not fitting that the kelipah benefit there from the food itself, which is holy; and so that it not accuse us over this, its portion was given to it in the mayim acharonim.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:66: And with this the statement ends, returning to say: therefore a person must not give the sustenance upon his table to that vomit and excrement, and all the more so within his innards — for this was already said at greater length above, that one must empty himself. And further, what does he mean by "and all the more so within his innards"? It is obvious that this is what we are dealing with.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:67: Rather, the matter is this: the sustenance that a person eats at his table indicates a supernal holiness upon it, for first he sanctifies his hands, as we shall explain in the corrections of the table; and afterward he blesses the blessing of "who brings forth bread" over the bread. The blessing over every fruit and over bread is to draw spirituality upon it from the great Name YHVH, who brings all into being, who gives soul and existence to all creatures, and He created this bread through all that is bound to the mentioned Name, for no creature is created except through the Cause of all who brings all into existence, as explained in Tikkunim (116a), these are his words: just as there is no partner to the letter vav of another letter, so it has no partner, for it is one and there is no second to it, one without number; it created all and there is no creator over it. And is there anyone who can create even a small gnat besides it? Rather, waters have the power to create trees and grasses, and they were created; but the Creator of the worlds created, and there is none who created it. Thus far his words. And through the blessing and the mention of the Name we arouse the supernal flow upon that bread or upon that fruit, just as at the beginning of its creation through the Name; thus in his eating he intends that the soul benefit from the spirituality of the great Name that has been clothed in that fruit, and so it has within it a portion of life, in the secret of (Nehemiah 9:6), "and You give life to them all." And likewise the waters called "living waters" — their secret is on this path, through the blessing we bless over them. And one who eats his food in this manner is called a living righteous one, and he cleaves to the supernal life, and he purifies the eating so as to give a portion to the soul. And we shall elaborate further on this matter below.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:68: And now in this there is good reason why it is not fitting to give from the holy food to the external [forces], and this is what was said above, "that he empty himself before he eats the sustenance of the pure table, for that sustenance he prepares — the Holy One, blessed be He, delights in it." These are two aspects: the first, concerning the food itself, which is holy; the second, concerning the table. And his saying "the Holy One, blessed be He, delights in it" points to the matter mentioned. And correspondingly he said two things: that one must give the residue and not the food — water, which is a washing, which is the filth that is not from the essence of the food on the table. And he returned to say "therefore," because it troubled him that after all we find that in the sacrifice they gave it a portion, regarding the limbs and fats, as explained in portion Terumah (141a), that the smoke would bend toward the north side; and so it should be fitting that at the table, called the altar, a portion of the food be given to it, and it would have been good that he not empty himself. To this he answered: "therefore a person must not give the sustenance upon his table to that vomit and excrement" — and his saying "upon his table" indicates that his table is the table that stands before the LORD, and it is not fitting to give from it to dogs called "vomit and excrement" — behold, even the vomit and excrement is excluded from it. And all the more so within his innards, for within him is holy — this being the holy soul, a portion of Him, blessed be He, and it is she who benefits from the food, and it is not fitting that the kelipah benefit there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:69: And the reason for the soul's sustenance is: for in truth it would be better that it not eat at all and subsist without eating altogether. But the matter is that, without doubt, before its coming into this world, it stands above and benefits from the radiance of the Shechinah, and the supernal beings — if they did not benefit from the radiance of the Shechinah, their existence would cease, for that illumination is the cause of their existence, as they explained in the Midrash HaZohar (portion Balak, 208a; portion Terumah, 156b). And of necessity they bring it down and clothe it in a body, and because of the cause of separation from the supernal source, it is impossible for it to benefit from the radiance of the Shechinah on account of the screen of the separating body. And Israel in the wilderness benefited somewhat from the radiance of the Shechinah — namely, the secret of the manna, which is supernal light that became materialized, as explained in the Zohar (ibid.), and therefore it was absorbed in the limbs (Yoma 75b) and was nourishment for body and soul as one. Afterward, however, they ate from the produce of the land — that is, the flow became materialized and thickened in the supernal land and in this land, which was not so with the manna, which did not become thickened in the supernal land, as it is written (Exodus 16:4), "Behold, I will rain" — it only passed through by way of transmission. Therefore it has a portion for man and a portion for the external [forces], namely the residue, the vomit and excrement. If so, a person is compelled to eat in order to give a spiritual portion to his soul, that it cleave and benefit somewhat from the radiance of the Shechinah through the ways we have mentioned.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:70: And there is some support for this in the matter of the four sustenances that Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, portion Beshalach, 61b), these are his words: he said that Israel, at the beginning of their departure from Egypt, ate matzah, which is the attribute of righteousness [tzedek]; afterward, when they were circumcised and uncovered [the circumcision], they merited to eat the manna, bread from heaven; then he said, the fellowship who occupy themselves with Torah were nourished from another, supernal place. What is it? As it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:12), "wisdom gives life to those who possess it" — a place higher still. Rabbi Elazar said to him: if so, why did their souls weaken more than the rest of the people of the world, when it should appear that they would be found with greater strength and power? He said to him: you have asked well. Come and see: all sustenance of the people of the world comes from above; that sustenance which comes from heaven and earth — this is the sustenance of the whole world, and it is coarse and thick sustenance. And that sustenance which comes from higher still is sustenance that comes with judgment, and from the place where judgment is found, is a sustenance still finer. The sustenance that was found for Israel at that time from the supernal place called "heaven" is a sustenance still finer, which enters more into the soul than anything, and is more separated from the body, and is called "the contemptible bread" [lechem hakelokel]. The sustenance higher than all is the sustenance of the fellowship, those who occupy themselves with Torah, who eat the sustenance of ruach and neshamah, and do not eat the sustenance of the body at all — and this is from the place higher and more precious than all, called Chochmah [Wisdom]. Because of this, the body of the fellowship is weaker than that of the rest of the world, since they do not eat the sustenance of the body at all, but eat the sustenance of ruach and neshamah, from a place distant and precious above all; and therefore that finest of the fine sustenance is more than all. Fortunate is their portion — this is what is written, "wisdom gives life to those who possess it": fortunate is the portion of the body that is able to be nourished by the sustenance of the soul. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:71: One should not interpret his statement regarding Torah scholars, that they do not eat the sustenance of the body at all, to mean that they do not eat at all — for we find that they did eat, and he says further below (62b): Rabbi Yesa would not prepare his meal every day until he had made his petition before the Holy One, blessed be He; he said, I will not prepare a meal until it is given from the King's house. After making his petition before the Holy One, blessed be He, he would wait an hour and say, "now is the time it is given from the King's house" — from then on they would prepare the meal. And this is the way of those who fear the Holy One, blessed be He, fearing sin. Thus far his words. And although they explained in portion Shemot in the Zohar (15a) that Rashbi, peace be upon him, and his companions stood two days without eating because they were occupied with Torah, not knowing whether it was day or night — nevertheless, certainly afterward they ate. And it would be fitting, since Torah is their sustenance, that they not be nourished by physical food at all; so we must understand what is meant by "they do not eat the sustenance of the body at all."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:72: However, the plain meaning of the matter is this: the sustenance — meaning the supernal flow — is drawn into this physical food that a person eats, according to the level of the person's soul; and even though the wise man and the ignorant man both eat this measure of bread, or the measure of one meal, each one draws his nourishment from the level of his soul, from the place at which he holds, and accordingly it will be thick and coarse, or fine. And this is what is meant by "the body of the fellowship is weaker than that of the rest of the world, since they do not eat the sustenance of the body at all" — the intent being that even though they eat the measure of a meal like the rest of the people, the body will be weak, because the spiritual flow drawn into that food is fine, and it is the sustenance of the soul entirely.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:73: And one should not interpret this to mean that because most Torah scholars are poor and their eating is scant, and that scant amount is the eating of the soul — as in the case of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, for whom a kav of carobs sufficed from Sabbath eve to Sabbath eve (Berachot 17b) — for it says simply "the fellowship," without qualification. And so he further says below, regarding the division of the four sustenances (62a), that he said: the holy and precious sustenance, the sustenance of ruach and neshamah, is the sustenance of the distant, supernal, and precious-above-all place — it is the sustenance of the fellowship who occupy themselves with Torah, and it is the sustenance that comes from supernal Chochmah. And why is this place different? Because Torah issues from supernal Chochmah, and those who occupy themselves with Torah enter into the very root of the source; therefore their sustenance comes from that holy, supernal place. Rabbi Elazar came and kissed his hands and said, fortunate is my portion that I stand upon these matters; fortunate is the portion of the righteous who occupy themselves with Torah day and night, for it earns them merit in this world and in the World to Come, as it is written (Deuteronomy 30:20), "for it is your life and the length of your days." Thus far his words. And the meaning is: "your life" in this world, and "length of days" in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 15:74: And likewise, there were several Torah scholars who were wealthy, like Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom (Yoma 35b); if so, did the wealthy Torah scholar lose out in not having his sustenance drawn from above? And likewise Rabbi Pinchas appears to have been wealthy, as is evident in the Zohar (portion Acharei Mot, end of 59). And we also find Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon, peace be upon him, of whom they said in the chapter "One Who Hires Workers" (Bava Metzia 84b) that he would eat sixty kinds of food when he was ill. Rather, certainly whether the flow drawn into the food when a person eats is coarse and thick or fine [depends on the person]: for the rest of the people, a coarse and thick flow is drawn, which is the sustenance of the body; and for Torah scholars, a fine flow is drawn from above for the sustenance of the soul, as explained. This is the meaning of (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" — meaning that the righteous man's eating is not directed at the health of his body and its being strong, but at the satisfaction of his soul, in order to give sustenance to his soul, since the supernal flow is drawn into that food, and through this his soul is satisfied. And certainly, through the prayer they would pray over their sustenance, as we have copied above regarding Rabbi Yesa, who would say, "now is the time it is given from the King's house" — the flow of the soul would be fine and spiritual; and this is "from the King's house," namely the Shechinah, which has already received the supernal flow, the sustenance of Torah scholars, to bestow upon them, which is not so for the rest of the people. And likewise through the intent of the eating, as explained above.
